kept.heading: CHATGPT DEFAULTS TO BRANDED SEARCH FOR "X BEST SOFTWARE" QUERIES (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: ChatGPT often starts product searches from a preselected set of brands it already associates with a category, making category eligibility more important than traditional SEO rankings. In one example, its first search for enterprise AI agent platforms already included Microsoft, Salesforce, Google, ServiceNow, IBM, and AWS before any neutral market scan. Challenger brands need repeated category association through owned content, comparison pages, third-party validation, analyst coverage, customer proof, and clear product messaging to enter these default vendor sets. Research suggests that appearing in ChatGPT's generated search query can be worth about 33 times more than simply being discoverable.
kept.article_text:
Title: ChatGPT Defaults to Branded Search for "X Best Software"

URL Source: https://marketingadvice.substack.com/p/chatgpt-defaults-to-branded-search

Published Time: 2026-08-17T13:09:25+00:00

Markdown Content:
1.   **Microsoft Copilot Studio** — best default if you are a Microsoft 365/Azure shop.

2.   **Salesforce Agentforce** — best if revenue, support, and CRM workflows are the main target.

3.   **ServiceNow AI Agents** — best for IT, HR, risk, and enterprise service workflows.

4.   **AWS Bedrock AgentCore** or **Google Vertex/Gemini Agent Platform** — best for developer-built agents on cloud infrastructure.

5.   **UiPath** — best if the company already has RPA/process automation maturity.

6.   **LangGraph/LangSmith** — best if your engineering team wants maximum control and portability.

I found **16 unique web search queries** in the network log:

1.   `2026 enterprise AI agent platform builders Microsoft Copilot Studio Salesforce Agentforce Google Vertex AI Agent Builder ServiceNow AI Agents IBM watsonx Orchestrate AWS Bedrock Agents comparison`

2.   `Gartner enterprise AI agents platforms 2025 2026 agentic AI platforms`

3.   `Forrester wave agentic AI platforms 2025 enterprise AI agents`

4.   `Microsoft Copilot Studio autonomous agents enterprise governance documentation 2026 site:microsoft.com`

5.   `Salesforce Agentforce enterprise AI agents features official 2026 site:salesforce.com`

6.   `Google Vertex AI Agent Builder official agents enterprise 2026 site:cloud.google.com`

7.   `ServiceNow AI Agents official enterprise 2026 site:servicenow.com`

8.   `AWS Bedrock Agents official enterprise AI agents 2026 site:aws.amazon.com`

9.   `IBM watsonx Orchestrate AI agent builder official 2026 site:ibm.com`

10.   `UiPath AI agents official enterprise 2026 site:uipath.com`

11.   `OpenAI AgentKit enterprise agents official 2026 site:openai.com`

12.   `Workday Sana enterprise AI agents official 2026 site:workday.com OR site:sana.ai`

13.   `Sana AI Workday enterprise AI agent platform official 2026`

14.   `LangGraph Platform enterprise AI agents official 2026 site:langchain.com`

15.   `CrewAI Enterprise AI agents official 2026 site:crewai.com`

16.   `Microsoft AutoGen enterprise AI agents official 2026 site:microsoft.com OR site:github.io`

ChatGPT already knew these brands were strong “enterprise AI platform” entities:

**Microsoft Copilot Studio, Salesforce Agentforce, Google Vertex AI Agent Builder, ServiceNow AI Agents, IBM watsonx Orchestrate, and AWS Bedrock Agents.**

ChatGPT did not start with a neutral market scan first. It generated those brands as a **pre-seeded set of vendor options**:

The log shows the very first web query was already preloaded with those vendors:

> `2026 enterprise AI agent platform builders Microsoft Copilot Studio Salesforce Agentforce Google Vertex AI Agent Builder ServiceNow AI Agents IBM watsonx Orchestrate AWS Bedrock Agents comparison`

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tZlb!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F35416bcc-7990-4611-949b-ee0fc4e46bb4_1438x1138.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tZlb!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F35416bcc-7990-4611-949b-ee0fc4e46bb4_1438x1138.png)

Answer engines create vendor shortlists based on pre-seeded / pre-determined entity knowledge.

In this example, ChatGPT did not perform a neutral category level search like you would expect to happen in traditional Google SEO.

It generated a pre-determined shortlist from the brands it already associated with **“enterprise AI agent platforms.”**

That is why Microsoft, Salesforce, Google, ServiceNow, IBM, and AWS were part of the default branded search — **[because AI search rewards category winners while everyone else has to fight their way in](https://marketingadvice.substack.com/p/ai-search-rewards-category-leaders)**.

The strategic takeaway is that **[no amount of GEO hacking](https://marketingadvice.substack.com/p/geo-is-a-reputation-problem-not-a)** is going to fix this.

The challenger brand would need to become part of the default seed set for these themes in order to get recommended by ChatGPT:

1.   **“enterprise AI agent builder”**

2.   **“low-code AI agent builder”**

3.   **“agentic application development platform”**

4.   **“enterprise AI agent orchestration platform”**

That requires owned content, comparison pages, third-party corroboration, analyst/PR language, customer proof, and structured product messaging that repeatedly puts any challenger within the same category neighborhood as those preferred vendors.

I concede this is not a full-blown study, but it’s an important anecdote.

I’ve manually tested and checked hundreds of answer recommendations from ChatGPT and its the same output every time — I just don’t have the energy to produce a study that reflects a statistically significant dataset.

If you want something more scientific, I’d recommend **[checking out Suganthan’s post here](https://suganthan.com/blog/chatgpt-decides-before-it-searches/)** which is more of a “proper” study with dozens more examples and fantastic ChatGPT audits.

His post outlines 4 strategic implications that I agree with:

1.   **ChatGPT writes its own search queries, and you can read them.**

2.   **Those queries already contain brands nobody previously mentioned.**

3.   **Being in that query is worth about 33 times more than being findable.**

4.   **Once you’re in, a second and much harsher filter decides who gets cited.**

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!me0l!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1758317d-65f5-428c-b9c8-d5bc44f6bdfd_1536x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!me0l!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1758317d-65f5-428c-b9c8-d5bc44f6bdfd_1536x1024.png)

kept.blurb: The IAB's updated framework gives brands, agencies, publishers, and technology partners practical triggers for disclosing AI-generated or AI-assisted text, images, video, audio, synthetic voices, digital twins, and consumer interactions. It also aims to prevent disclosure fatigue by avoiding labels when AI use is not materially relevant to the consumer experience.

kept.heading: OPENAI LAUNCHES A SAFER CHATGPT FOR TEENS (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: ChatGPT for Teens has added safety measures and tools designed to reduce AI-assisted cheating. The experience includes Study Mode, which guides students through problems instead of giving quick answers, plus quizzes, learning visualizations, homework reminders, and parental controls. OpenAI is also adding age-appropriate content protections and partnering with CodeAI to teach teens how to use and question AI.
kept.article_text:
Title: OpenAI launches a safer ChatGPT for teens — years after teens started using it

URL Source: https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/18/openai-launches-a-safer-chatgpt-for-teens-years-after-teens-started-using-it/

Published Time: 2026-08-18T13:50:30+00:00

Markdown Content:
After [numerous](https://techcrunch.com/2026/06/01/florida-sues-openai-sam-altman-in-first-of-its-kind-lawsuit-over-violent-incidents/)[lawsuits](https://techcrunch.com/2025/11/23/chatgpt-told-them-they-were-special-their-families-say-it-led-to-tragedy/) over AI chatbots’ lack of safety measures, leading to teens’ suicides and other mental health concerns, OpenAI on Monday [announced](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-for-teens/) the launch of ChatGPT for Teens. The new product promises to include additional safety measures, as well as address the educational crisis of ChatGPT-assisted cheating in schools.

On the educational side, ChatGPT for Teens introduces a new Study Mode feature and other tools designed to encourage teen users to engage their curiosity and work through problems, not just get quick answers.

As OpenAI explains [in a blog post](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-for-teens/), the Study Mode option will give teens guiding questions and step-by-step support to help them understand the material. Meanwhile, the teen experience will also include homework reminders that appear when a teen appears to be trying to cheat, instead of understanding the material. The AI chatbot will then push the teen to use Study Mode instead.

The app will also support quizzes and learning visualizations, and controls that allow parents or guardians to decide when Study Mode is enabled by default, the company says.

Still, it’s not clear how difficult it will be for teens to escape these new systems if they decide not to cooperate. Teens are incredibly adept at working around parental controls and other attempts to lock down digital experiences. Until ChatGPT’s teen mode can be put to more strenuous tests, it’s unclear how difficult it will be to work around these safety measures in reality.

![Image 1](https://techcrunch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Still-02-teenStudyHours__2_.webp?w=680)

**Image Credits:**OpenAI

There’s also the question as to why these protections weren’t part of ChatGPT from the beginning. The AI chatbot first arrived in late 2022 and scaled to [900 million weekly users](https://techcrunch.com/2026/02/27/chatgpt-reaches-900m-weekly-active-users/) before meaningful safeguards designed specifically for teenage users were added.

OpenAI says the age-appropriate protections will now be on by default in ChatGPT for Teens, which are designed to reduce exposure to harmful or developmentally inappropriate content. These measures are based on OpenAI’s [Under-18 Principles in our Model Spec](https://openai.com/index/updating-model-spec-with-teen-protections/), which the company claims to be informed by “developmental science and guidance from experts.”

Parents will also be able to use the family tools and parental controls [previously introduced](https://openai.com/index/introducing-parental-controls/) to manage settings, receive safety notifications, and set Quiet Hours, among other things.

OpenAI announced a partnership with CodeAI to help teens learn more about AI, including how it works, how to direct it or question it, and how to use it. In the classroom, OpenAI already offers [ChatGPT for Teachers](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-for-teachers/) to help provide schools with institution-managed access to AI and support.

kept.heading: STOP MAKING THE CREATOR THE HERO: A TALENT AGENCY FOUNDER'S HYPE CHECK (51 MINUTE PODCAST)
kept.blurb: Mega-influencers and celebrities still drive results, but brands often use them incorrectly. This podcast breaks down how to negotiate celebrity rates, when to use top-of-funnel versus bottom-of-funnel creators, and how whitelisting can turn creator content into a performance channel. It also covers why long-term creator partnerships aren't always the best approach and how brands can land major talent without paying traditional talent fees.
kept.article_text:
Title: Tinashe Chaponda (Sosani) - Stop Making the Creator the Hero: A Talent Agency Founder's Hype Check - Influence Weekly

URL Source: https://influenceweekly.buzzsprout.com/2245094/episodes/19644697-tinashe-chaponda-sosani-stop-making-the-creator-the-hero-a-talent-agency-founder-s-hype-check

Everyone in the creator economy has decided mega-influencers and celebrities are washed up — that follower count doesn't matter anymore. Tinashe Chaponda, founder of Sosani, says that's exactly backwards. In this episode, he breaks down why big names still move the needle, and why the real problem is brands don't know how to work with them.

Tinashe pulls back the curtain on how top talent agencies actually negotiate celebrity rates, why "whitelisting" content is the difference between an organic post and a real sales driver, and why the industry's obsession with long-term creator partnerships might be doing more harm than good.

**In this episode:**

kept.heading: WHY TYLER SPEEGLE TREATS HIS CREATOR BUSINESS LIKE A MARKETER WOULD (5 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Creator Tyler Speegle uses his marketing background to treat content like an A/B test, analyzing what drives views and iterating on it. He also turned repeated audience questions about his homemade seasonings into his own product line. The move gave him a new revenue stream while creating conflicts with competing sponsorships. He now uses content to drive product launches, including seasonal releases and a planned cookbook.
kept.article_text:
Title: Why Tyler Speegle Treats His Creator Business Like A Marketer Would

URL Source: https://www.netinfluencer.com/why-tyler-speegle-treats-his-creator-business-like-a-marketer-would/

Published Time: 2026-08-18T08:02:59-04:00

Markdown Content:
Tyler Speegle is a marketer by training and a lifestyle creator by practice. Based in Birmingham, Alabama, he launched [Tyler Growth Life](https://thegrowthlife.com/) as a cooking and family content brand for the parent who dreads the question of what to make for dinner. His content does not feature elaborate plating or competitive technique. It features meals, kids in the background, and the argument that ordinary weeknight rituals are worth paying attention to.

Tyler Growth Life spans [TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@tylergrowthlife?lang=en), [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/tylergrowthlife/?hl=en), and [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/@TylerGrowthLife), where he repurposes footage across all three. In December 2025, he extended the brand into a product line, launching three seasonings: Cast Iron Coffee, Southwest Smoke, and Golden Hour Garlic. A cowboy butter blend followed for Father’s Day 2026. He has since signed with a book agent and is developing a cookbook proposal.

The philosophy underlying all of it is less about cooking than about pace. “To me, it’s more than just the food,” Tyler says. “It’s like the whole experience of enjoying the moment.”

## **The Marketing Test That Built a Cooking Channel**

Tyler spent just over a decade in marketing before his brand existed. He started with part-time blogging, moved into copywriting at a nonprofit where he was later promoted to digital marketing director, and most recently served as a growth marketer at a B2B venture studio. The discipline across those years was the same: understand what draws people in and why.

That reflex applied directly to content. When his lifestyle and cooking videos began generating views in the hundreds of thousands consistently, rather than the few hundred he had seen from earlier experiments, he analyzed the shift the same way he would have analyzed a digital ad campaign. “When you see something that worked, analyze what about that worked,” Tyler says.

He describes the method in A/B testing terms: “You have something that worked. That’s your control. Now I’m going to basically do a test of, if I do that same thing, change a variable here or there, whether it’s what I’m cooking or the environment or the pacing.”

He built this way without paid advertising, noting that the marketing instinct let him identify what was resonating and iterate faster than trial and error alone would have allowed.

Before signing with Currents Management, Tyler had reached out to brands directly, searching LinkedIn for contacts and pitching his view counts. The outreach rarely converted. With management, alignment came faster. His first major deal landed with Benchmade, a knife company he had already used and followed. He added affiliate income through Amazon and LTK after noticing his audience was asking about the tools and products visible in his videos.

## **When the Comments Became a Product Order**

The seasoning business was built from questions Tyler was already fielding in his comments. For years, he had been mixing his own blends at home rather than buying commercial seasonings, which he found too sweet, too full of fillers, or too spicy for his kids. He cooked with those blends on camera, and the audience noticed.

“I kept having people ask me, ‘What are you putting in that?'” Tyler recalls. The volume of those questions, combined with a discomfort about recommending other companies’ products as if they were his own, pushed him toward manufacturing. “I don’t have control over their flavor profile,” he says. “And I don’t have control over the customer service.”

![Image 1](blob:http://localhost/b44a94e66bffa08ab58504530f1ddff7)
Product development proved less straightforward than the concept. Getting Golden Hour Garlic right took five iterations with his manufacturer: too much paprika made the blend bitter, salt ratios needed adjustment, and different smoked paprika varieties produced different colors and textures. “Launching three at one time was a big undertaking,” Tyler says.

The [cowboy butter blend](https://thegrowthlife.com/products/cowboy-butter), launched for Father’s Day 2026, took fewer iterations because Tyler had learned from the first round. The product compresses a recipe that typically requires fresh garlic, Dijon mustard, parsley, and lemon into a single powder. “You just take the powder, mix it with some butter, and you have cowboy butter almost instantly,” he says.

## **Owning the Product Means Turning Down Certain Deals**

Building a seasoning brand created a category conflict Tyler had not fully anticipated. Brands that might once have been natural sponsorship partners became complicated to work with. “It can be kind of complicated to promote someone else’s seasoning,” Tyler says. “I’ve stepped away from those kinds of brand partnerships.”

For all other food and drink collaborations, his filter is brand alignment over revenue. He uses the product, believes in what the company stands for, and can speak to it genuinely. “People can tell if you don’t use this product,” he says. “I don’t want to promote brands that I don’t really know much about.”

The decision to exit a sponsorship category comes with a cost Tyler does not minimize. “The return on having a seasoning brand has definitely been worth it in the long run,” he says.

Physical product also introduced operational challenges. Storage, logistics, and customer service at scale do not work the way digital content does. “I did not realize just how not easy it is to sell a physical product,” Tyler says. He hired his cousin early as a part-time customer service assistant. “There’s no way I would have had the time or the capacity to truly treat every customer the way I want them to be treated,” he says.

His next marketing step, he notes, is scaling distribution beyond himself, seeding the product with other creators.

![Image 2](blob:http://localhost/f3a16eb94533235f35de1ae8674ede8c)
## **The Case for Giving Audiences Something to Hold**

Tyler’s push to make something tangible is a reaction to the rise of AI-generated cooking content. “There are AI content creators where everything is completely AI, the person, the food,” he says. “It’s not awesome now, but it will only get better and more real.”

Against that trajectory, he notes that a physical product does something a video cannot. “I think the real personal connection that you can kind of double down on by giving something to somebody that they can hold in their hands is going to matter even more and more as AI becomes more and more real,” he says.

Tyler’s argument extends to search, where AI tools are becoming, in his view, “the new way people Google.” When a viewer later searches for something they saw in one of his videos, an AI search tool needs somewhere to send them. “Search is very different than it used to be,” he says. “I think by having an actual website where a product is located, where people can check out, that’s definitely something people have to think about.”

## **The Next Product Is the Long Game**

Tyler’s plans for the rest of 2026 follow the same logic he applies to content: time the release to something people already care about. A fall seasoning launch is designed around football season and outdoor cooking. A holiday launch follows, aimed at baking and festive meals. He calls both themed launches, a structure that makes the product and the content part of the same moment rather than separate campaigns.

He is also working with a book agent on a cookbook proposal, a project his audience requested for around two years before he started the process. “I’m really excited again to get something tangible in people’s hands that takes the content beyond just the screen,” he says.

The two tracks reflect a consistent position: brand partnerships produce immediate returns, and the product businesses are a longer investment in an audience that knows him primarily through a screen.

“I hope that when people start following me, watching my content, that it leaves them with a positive feeling of, ‘Oh, I can actually enjoy the life I have,’” he says. “We all move really fast. We’re all really distracted. We all have a lot going on and, if you’re not careful, you’ll miss the beauty of everyday life.”

kept.blurb: Anthropic's new watermarking works by quietly changing which word Claude picks when two options seem equally good. It swaps in a hidden key instead of plain randomness, so the pattern stays invisible to readers but detectable later. The company treats that kind of choice as low stakes, the difference between grey and overcast. However, word choice for a human writer usually carries intent, mood, and context that a statistical model can't see. Anthropic says internal testing found no measurable drop in quality or creativity from the change. The bigger problem isn't the watermark itself. It's that a company building writing tools thinks words are interchangeable in the first place.
kept.article_text:
Title: Anthropic’s Text Watermarking Proves AI Companies Do Not Care at All About Writing

URL Source: https://www.404media.co/anthropics-text-watermarking-proves-ai-companies-do-not-care-at-all-about-writing/

Published Time: 2026-08-18T15:54:15.000Z

Markdown Content:
Earlier this month, Anthropic announced that future versions of Claude will generate text that includes watermarks showing it was AI-generated. At the time, Anthropic did not explain how this would work, leaving us to speculate on the podcast: Would it somehow encode this into the text? Include invisible characters? Do something with the metadata? We now know, thanks to a blog post over the weekend, that Anthropic will do this by changing how its AI writes altogether.

“Nothing is added to the text and there are no hidden characters,” Anthropic wrote [in that company blog post](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-text-watermark?ref=404media.co). “The difference between watermarked and un-watermarked text will not be distinguishable to readers.” The way it will work, the post explained, is that Anthropic will subtly alter the word choices in AI-generated text in a way that is only known to Anthropic and its algorithms. Anthropic will know the watermarking algorithm, which will change “the source of the randomness used to pick among words” and thus can write a tool to detect whether something has been AI-generated.

This research and approach is interesting in a data science kind of way, but Anthropic’s layperson explanation for how this will work shows how little the company thinks about the craft of writing or the subtle differences between words a human author might want to use to convey their thoughts.

Anthropic asks us to consider the difference between two sentences: “Take the sentence ‘The weather today was cold and…’. The next word is very unlikely to be ‘sugary.’ But it is quite likely to be ‘overcast’ or ‘grey.’ Under most circumstances, it doesn’t matter much to the reader which of these latter two words the model ultimately chooses—the meaning of the sentence is largely the same either way. In cases like this, the choice is settled by a random number,” Anthropic writes. “Watermarking uses low-stakes choices like these—which occur many times over a piece of generated text—to leave a pattern in Claude’s responses. That pattern is undetectable to the reader, but _is_ detectable to anyone who has a key that encodes it. When watermarking is used, choices are still made at random, but the _source_ of the randomness is different.”

Anyone who has written anything would, I hope, understand that the difference between the sentences “The weather today was cold and grey” and “The weather today was cold and overcast” are sometimes “low stakes,” as Anthropic describes, but not always. “Grey,” and “overcast” are different words, and there are any number of reasons why a human author might pick one over the other in a given context. In this example, however, Anthropic’s algorithm sees these words as totally interchangeable and thus its watermarking algorithm has decided that it can “nudge” the word choice one way or the other for the purposes of watermarking.

Anthropic continues: “Instead of using an arbitrary random number generator to pick the next word, watermarking uses the key and a few words that come before to settle what word the model should pick. That is, the words that Claude picks are still random, but now, one can check the sequence of words and see if it’s consistent with the choices Claude would make if it was using the key. If it is, one can assign a probability that the text was generated by Claude.”

Anthropic claims “Watermarking does not impact the quality of Claude’s output. To a reader, a watermarked response is indistinguishable from an unwatermarked one,” and that “in internal testing, we’ve seen no impact of watermarking on the content, level of creativity, or readability of Claude’s text.”

People are quite mad about Anthropic’s watermarking system, and understandably so. Synonyms are sometimes interchangeable, but not always, as is [pointed out in this excellent essay by John Gruber of Daring Fireball](https://daringfireball.net/2026/08/anthropics_watermark_text_adulteration_in_claude_is_a_perversion_of_writing?ref=404media.co), and by journalism academic Jeff Jarvis, [in which he claims Anthropic “devalues writing](https://medium.com/whither-news/words-matter-damnit-fc883733a729?ref=404media.co).” In making this choice, “Anthropic declares words fungible, language random, choice meaningless,” Jarvis writes.

When I sat down to write this post, I was mad because it seems like Anthropic is putting its thumb on the scale, messing with the outputs of its machine and saying that the resulting text is qualitatively just the same as the other AI text it was probably going to output. But as I began writing this, I realized that my problem is not necessarily with text watermarking but with AI-generated text altogether. It does not matter to me, necessarily, whether the output of Claude’s garbage AI text is one way or is a slightly different way. But it does matter to me that AI data scientists at huge tech companies think that word choice doesn’t matter, or that it is possible to statistically use synonyms wherever without fucking with the meaning of a sentence.

Throughout the blog post, Anthropic describes the act of writing as being akin to a probabilistic game of chance. In Anthropic’s own words, its writing is sometimes the result of an “arbitrary random number generator,” and “random” whenever its systems encounter a situation where its tool believes, based on pattern recognition, that the choice between several possible next words isn’t all that important. That may be true for LLM garbage, but is not true for the human experience of writing, which is why human writing almost always _feels_ different than AI writing.

This watermarking approach, and Anthropic’s blog post about it, highlights something that should already be clear about a company that famously scanned and destroyed huge numbers of printed books and has trained its LLMs on stolen content: Anthropic does not care about the craft or effort of writing, and sees words as fungible and unimportant. Anthropic says it is making this change as part of the European Union’s new AI regulations, which are well-intentioned but problematic. While it can definitely be useful to have additional ways of detecting AI-generated content, the carelessness with which Anthropic has announced this decision highlights the broader problem with using LLMs to write: They are, as Anthropic notes, probabilistic tools that do not “write” in the way that humans do, rather, they mimic their training data which is, by definition, things that have already happened and been ingested.

Contrast this with how Anthropic sees code, something where it says an “exact output is required.” In writing, meanwhile, Anthropic suggests different words are often “equally good.” Over and over again, Anthropic and the researchers who work on this type of watermarking claim that text can be “nudged” in this way without being noticeable to humans or without impacting “quality.”

But it is worth noting that the people judging the “quality” of the AI-generated outputs are either data scientists or people asking AI tools to do their writing for them, not, say, people who care about reading or writing. The scientific paper that Anthropic [cites was done by Google researchers](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08025-4?ref=404media.co) on a Google watermarking tool called “SynthID,” which Anthropic’s watermarking is based on.

In the SynthID study, quality was assessed by randomly putting watermarking on some Gemini outputs, then asking Gemini users to either thumbs-up or thumbs-down the response: “A random fraction of queries were routed to a watermarked model and an equivalent number to the unwatermarked counterpart. The Gemini user interface allows users to provide feedback on model responses via a thumbs-up (good response) and a thumbs-down (bad response). We analysed approximately 20 million watermarked and unwatermarked responses and computed the thumbs-up and thumbs-down rates (both as a fraction of the total number of thumbs-up and thumbs-down feedback received). We found that the thumbs-up rate for the two models differed by 0.01%.”

I hope it is clear to anyone who has clicked on this article that asking someone who asked a chatbot something to thumbs up or thumbs down a response is not a very good way of assessing the “quality” of “writing.” The other human assessment that Google did was to ask people to assess side-by-side watermarked and unwatermarked text for quality. Here are examples given in an appendix of the study; apparently people did not really have a preference one way or the other:

[![Image 1](https://storage.ghost.io/c/0f/76/0f76b548-bc58-4f25-abc3-3f5ebca07da4/content/images/2026/08/data-src-image-0a971f0c-8c38-40c1-aa4d-5d8260c5c3e6-1.png)](https://storage.ghost.io/c/0f/76/0f76b548-bc58-4f25-abc3-3f5ebca07da4/content/images/2026/08/data-src-image-0a971f0c-8c38-40c1-aa4d-5d8260c5c3e6-1.png)
One could argue that these passages are two different ways of explaining something, yes. But they are definitively _not_ the “same,” and it is unclear to any reader why one version is one way and the other version is another way. Why did the LLM write “respiratory failure” in one example and “cessation of breathing” in the other? The answer for both is an “arbitrary random number generator” and proprietary black box algorithmic weighting systems controlled by the AI company. In the watermarked version there’s been an additional “nudging” or messing with the machine that’s already just a pattern matcher.

The point is, there is no conscious thought or decision-making process happening here, so perhaps watermarked AI text is not all that much more offensive than regular AI text. But to see it laid out in such stark terms by the companies building these machines shows how little they actually care about writing. If you asked me, on the other hand, why I used one word instead of another, I might not be able to tell you exactly why, but I could probably explain to you what I was going for, the style of writing I do, my intended audience, my mood that day, whether my heart was racing or not, where I was, what I was doing, what I did earlier that morning and what I did later that day. Maybe it was a word my third grade teacher used all the time or which I read in an article last week or is an inside joke with my friends or which I have recently become obsessed with or tend to overuse. Why I wrote what I wrote or why I did anything at all is the result of my some mix of human experiences dating back to when I first acquired language as a baby and continuing on to this very moment that I may or may not be able to explain, but which result in a certain style of writing that is _mine_.

This is the case even when I’m working fast or carelessly dashing off text messages, when the thoughts just kind of flow from my brain to my fingers to my keyboard where I don’t know if what I’m saying is making sense at all but is probably legible because it’s coming from a human brain and not a random number generator.

This is why short passages of [AI-generated text feel soulless and generic](https://www.404media.co/your-ai-use-is-breaking-my-brain/), as we have written about repeatedly. And there are many AI tools that use AI to make AI writing seem _less_ generic (yo dawg, we heard you like AI so we put AI in your AI) by using synonyms that are supposed to make a passage sound more human — or less plagiarized — by picking words that are less commonly used. The text outputted by these tools, which are called “spinners” or “humanizers” are often just as uncanny and weird as AI writing itself. Or, when applied to things where, to use Anthropic’s own language, “an exact output is required” such as quotes in a news article, the output is often factually inaccurate, libelous, or just plain garbage.

About the author

Jason is a cofounder of 404 Media. He was previously the editor-in-chief of Motherboard. He loves the Freedom of Information Act and surfing.

![Image 2: Jason Koebler](https://storage.ghost.io/c/0f/76/0f76b548-bc58-4f25-abc3-3f5ebca07da4/content/images/2023/08/404-jason-01-copy.jpeg)

TikTok has launched a new [artificial intelligence-powered introduction tool](https://www.threads.com/@oncescuradu/post/DcMCCCFDDpD)within the TikTok Live composer, which will generate a summary of the live host and the focus of their broadcast, which they can then share with viewers.

![Image 22: TikTok AI intro](https://imgproxy.divecdn.com/jgLO3gZUt2LCLbg1rFmxQtfcSW3eMN1iCzHAhGCSxPw/g:ce/rs:fit:1600:0/Z3M6Ly9kaXZlc2l0ZS1zdG9yYWdlL2RpdmVpbWFnZS90aWt0b2tfYWlfaW50cm8ucG5n.webp)

As shown in this sequence, shared on Threads by app researcher Radu Oncescu, live creators on TikTok can tap a button to generate an audience intro summary, which will provide additional context for viewers.

Which could be helpful, having easy access to a description that’s specifically aligned with live streams. But then again, based on the example above, it’s not entirely clear how accurate that description will be, nor how the AI-powered process generates these descriptions.

Really, it feels like another AI tool that doesn’t help much, doesn’t move the needle in a significant way and isn’t really a good use of the water and power resources required to power such options.

Increasingly, social platforms and AI providers are trying to find new ways to use the tech to enhance the user experience. But for a technology that’s being touted as the next major evolution in human history, actual use cases for such should probably be more evident.

It doesn’t seem like a great endorsement of the unending power and utility of the latest AI tools that apps are using it to replace processes that really aren’t that difficult for regular users. In fact, in some cases, the tasks that they’re looking to replace are some of the more enjoyable parts of the human experience.

Creating things is a joy, an expression of the human spirit. We don’t need AI to replace that. Choosing what to eat, where to travel, communicating with kids: None of these things require AI intervention.

Yet, more features are being pushed out, prompting users to automate basic tasks, which won’t save them a lot of time and are unlikely to improve their experience.

Writing a social media bio is about sharing something personal, and while there is a use case for creating a more compelling bio to lure more viewers in, surely this is not a necessary AI addition.

There are practical, valuable use cases for AI, with more and more being discovered every day. But things like this seem more confusing than beneficial.
